📜 'Of All That He Has' — why the Torah needed four separate exclusions, not just one
🤝 Can Priests and Levites Dedicate Their Own Property? — Rabbi Yehuda vs. Rabbi Shimon
👳 Who Receives a Dedication? — any priest for movables, but only the active watch for land
🐑 Dedicating What's Already Consecrated — vow-offerings, gift-offerings, and firstborn animals

overview.title: 📖 Overview: The Limits and Mechanics of Ḥerem
overview.subtitle: Arakhin 28a–28b
overview.hebrewSource: מַחֲרִים אָדָם מִצֹּאנוֹ וּמִבְּקָרוֹ, וּמֵעֲבָדָיו וּמִשִּׁפְחוֹתָיו הַכְּנַעֲנִים, וּמִשְּׂדֵה אֲחוּזָּתוֹ, וְאִם הֶחְרִים אֶת כּוּלָּם אֵינָם מוּחְרָמִים
overview.label: The scene:
overview.text: After finishing the auction mechanics of the previous chapter, the daf turns to a stronger, more absolute form of consecration: ḥerem, dedication for the priests. A new mishna sets its outer limit — one may dedicate part of his flocks, slaves, or ancestral field, but never everything, even for God's own sake. The Gemara traces this to four separate exclusions in a single verse, each independently necessary. It then asks who may dedicate at all (not property that isn't fully one's own — and priests and Levites are debated), who receives a dedication once made, and finally how one dedicates an item that is already consecrated for the altar, such as a vow-offering, a gift-offering, or a firstborn animal.

slides.title: 🔒 New Mishna: You May Not Dedicate EVERYTHING
slides.subtitle: Rabbi Eliezer's limit, and Rabbi Elazar ben Azarya's a fortiori extension

steps.content: 1️⃣ A person may dedicate some of his flock, cattle, Canaanite slaves, or ancestral field — but not all of any category
2️⃣ Rabbi Eliezer: if he dedicated ALL of a category, the dedication simply does not take effect
3️⃣ Rabbi Elazar ben Azarya's kal vachomer: if a person may not give even the Most High everything, all the more so he should be sparing with what he gives to other people

4️⃣ Practical difference: the Sages of Usha later enacted that charity should never exceed one-fifth of one's wealth — Rabbi Eliezer allows giving nearly all (keeping a token amount) to hekdesh; Rabbi Elazar ben Azarya caps it at a fifth even there

callout.label: A real test case:
callout.text: One man wished to give away more than a fifth of his wealth to charity; his colleague — Rabbi Yeshevav (or, some say, Rabbi Akiva) — stopped him from doing so.

slides.title: 📜 Why the Torah Needed Four Separate Exclusions
slides.subtitle: Leviticus 27:28: 'of all that he has... of man... of animal... of his ancestral field'

nodes.content: ❓ Why not just write 'of all that he has'? Why also spell out man, animal, and field separately?
💡 Without each: one might think only the general rule applies, but a person could still dedicate an ENTIRE single category — all his slaves, or all his animals, or all his field

columns.label: Slaves & field
columns.content: Both tied to livelihood — one might think both are equally protected without a separate verse for each

columns.label: Movable goods
columns.content: Without 'animal' as a third case, one might think livelihood-items alone are protected and ALL movables could still be dedicated

nodes.content: ✅ Bonus teaching from 'animal': one may dedicate only what he has permission to sell permanently — excluding a minor daughter (sellable only temporarily as a maidservant) or a purchased field (returns at the Jubilee)

slides.title: 🤝 Can Priests and Levites Dedicate Their Own Property?
slides.subtitle: New mishna: Rabbi Yehuda and Rabbi Shimon disagree, and Rebbi reconciles them

lines.speaker: R' Yehuda
lines.text: Neither priests nor Levites can dedicate their property. Priests can't, because dedications already belong to them as a priestly gift — you can't give someone their own thing. Levites can't either, since the Torah juxtaposes movable goods to land, and Levite land is inalienable ('their perpetual possession').

lines.speaker: R' Shimon
lines.text: Priests can't dedicate — same reason as R' Yehuda. But Levites CAN dedicate, since dedications are not theirs at all — I don't read that juxtaposition to land the same way.

lines.speaker: Rebbi's resolution
lines.text: Rabbi Yehuda's view fits land best (Levite fields truly are inalienable). Rabbi Shimon's view fits movable property best (Levites may freely dedicate that) — but even Rabbi Shimon concedes Levite land cannot be dedicated.

slides.title: 👳 Who Receives a Dedicated Item?
slides.subtitle: Movable property vs. land follow different rules — derived by verbal analogy
rows: 'Everything dedicated in Israel shall be yours' (Num. 18:14) — 'yours' broadly
Only the priestly watch currently serving in the Temple
Gezeirah shava 'to the priest'–'to the priest' from stolen property of a convert (Num. 5:8)
A field that reverts to priests at the Jubilee (unredeemed)
The watch serving when the Jubilee begins
Same principle — tied to active service
If the Jubilee begins on Shabbat (watch-rotation day)
The watch that is ending its service that day
Rav Ḥiyya bar Ami, in the name of Ḥulfana — since watches rotate only in the morning, and Jubilee begins with Rosh Hashana

slides.title: 🐑 Dedicating What's Already Consecrated
slides.subtitle: New mishna: dedications for priests need no redemption at all — and can even apply to sacrifices

boxes.title: General Dedications (Ḥerem)
items: Unlike Temple-maintenance consecration, ḥerem has no redemption — given directly to a priest, like teruma
R' Yehuda ben Beteira: unspecified dedication defaults to Temple maintenance (bedek habayit)
The Rabbis: unspecified dedication defaults to the priests directly

boxes.title: Dedicating Already-Sacred Animals
items: A vow-offering (e.g. 'a burnt-offering is upon me') → he owes its full value, since he must replace it
A gift-offering (e.g. 'this bull is a burnt-offering') → he owes only the 'benefit' — what someone would pay to sacrifice it, though not strictly permitted to
A firstborn animal, blemished or not → redeemed by assessing what an Israelite would pay a priest-relative to receive it

summary.principle: Dedication (ḥerem) for the priests is a stronger form of consecration than ordinary hekdesh — irredeemable, given directly like teruma — yet it too has firm limits: no one may dedicate everything he owns, only what he may permanently sell, and precise rules govern who may dedicate, who receives the gift, and how already-sacred animals fit into the category.

flowSteps.content: 🔒 A person may dedicate part, never all, of his flocks, slaves, or field — a fortiori true for ordinary charity
📜 Four separate scriptural exclusions guard against dedicating an entire category, each independently necessary

columns.content: 🤝 Priests can't dedicate (it's already theirs); Levites' land can't, but Rabbi Shimon allows their movables
👳 Movable dedications go to any priest; dedicated land goes only to the currently serving watch

flowSteps.content: 🐑 Dedicating one's own sacrifices: full value for a vow-offering, only its 'benefit' for a gift-offering
🎓 Key Principle: even the most absolute act of dedication to God still respects the boundary that a person may never surrender the entirety of his livelihood

quiz.q: According to Rabbi Eliezer in the new mishna, what happens if a person dedicates ALL of one category of his property, such as his entire flock?
o: The dedication takes full effect as usual
The dedication does not take effect at all
Only half of the flock becomes dedicated
He must add an additional animal to make it valid
quiz.e: Rabbi Eliezer rules that dedicating an entire category of property — all of one's flock, slaves, or field — is invalid; the dedication simply does not take effect, derived from the word 'notwithstanding' (akh) in Leviticus 27:28.

quiz.q: Why does the Torah need to separately exclude 'of man,' 'of animal,' and 'of his ancestral field,' rather than relying on the general phrase 'of all that he has'?
o: Because each word is purely stylistic with no legal significance
Because without each separate exclusion, one might think an entire single category (like all his slaves, or all his movable goods) could still be fully dedicated
Because the Torah always repeats phrases for emphasis alone
Because different categories require different priests to receive them
quiz.e: The Gemara explains that each exclusion is independently necessary: without 'of man,' one might think an entire category could still be wholly dedicated as long as the general rule was satisfied elsewhere, and so on for each category, including movable goods generally, via 'animal.'

quiz.q: How does Rebbi (Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi) reconcile the mishna's dispute between Rabbi Yehuda and Rabbi Shimon over whether Levites may dedicate their property?
o: He rules that neither opinion is correct
He says Rabbi Yehuda's view fits land (Levite land is inalienable) and Rabbi Shimon's view fits movable property (which Levites may freely dedicate)
He says both sages agree completely and there is no practical difference
He says the dispute applies only to priests, not Levites
quiz.e: Rebbi explains that Rabbi Yehuda's ruling that Levites cannot dedicate applies most accurately to land, since Levite fields are their inalienable perpetual possession, while Rabbi Shimon's more lenient ruling applies to movable property, which even Rabbi Shimon agrees Levites may dedicate.

quiz.q: According to the Gemara, who receives a field that a person dedicates (as opposed to movable property he dedicates)?
o: Any priest the donor personally chooses, exactly like movable property
Only the priestly watch that is currently serving in the Temple, derived by verbal analogy from the law of stolen property of a deceased convert
It must be sold and the proceeds split among all priests equally
It reverts automatically to the Temple treasury for maintenance
quiz.e: Unlike movable dedications, which go to any priest the donor wishes (per Numbers 18:14), a dedicated field goes specifically to the priestly watch currently serving in the Temple, derived via a gezeirah shava ('to the priest'–'to the priest') from the law of a convert's stolen property (Numbers 5:8).

quiz.q: What is the difference in how one dedicates a VOW-offering versus a GIFT-offering that is already consecrated, according to the new mishna?
o: There is no difference; both require the same payment
For a vow-offering he must give its full value (since he's obligated to replace it); for a gift-offering he gives only its 'benefit' — what someone would pay to sacrifice it
Vow-offerings cannot be dedicated at all
Gift-offerings require double payment compared to vow-offerings
quiz.e: Since a vow-offering (like 'a burnt-offering is incumbent upon me') obligates the person to replace the animal if lost, dedicating it requires paying its full value; a gift-offering (like 'this bull is a burnt-offering') carries no such replacement obligation, so only the assessed 'benefit' of sacrificing it is owed.
